                      UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                       
3                                                                        
                           DISTRICT OF NEVADA                            
4                                                                        
                                  * * *                                  
5                                                                        
    Luxx International, LLC and Wayde King,    Case No. 2:23-cv-00512-MMD-DJA 
6                                                                        
                   Plaintiffs,                                           
7                                                  Order                 
              v.                                                         
8                                                                        
    Pure Water Technologies; Tasty One, LLC;                             
9   Michael Kaplan; and Adam Kaplan,                                     

10                  Defendants.                                           

11                                                                        
12       Before the Court is Plaintiff Wayde King’s motion to compel Defendants Pure Water 
13  Technologies, Adam Kaplan, and Michael Kaplan to provide supplemental discovery responses 
14  and to pay King’s fees and costs associated with bringing the motion.  (ECF No. 31).  Also before 
15  the Court is Defendants Adam Kaplan and Michael Kaplan’s countermotion for a protective order 
16  (ECF No. 35) and Defendant Pure Water Technologies’ joinder to that motion (ECF No. 36).  
17  Because the Court finds that a motion to compel is unnecessary, but that a blanket protective 
18  order containing King’s proposed language is appropriate, it denies King’s motion to compel and 
19  grants in part and denies in part the Kaplan Defendants’ counter-motion for protective order. 
20  I.   Background.                                                      
21       King argues that, on the day Defendants’ discovery responses were due, Defendants 
22  asserted that they needed a protective order in place to respond.1  After discussions regarding the 
23  terms of that order fell apart, King filed the instant motion.  In addition to compelling Defendants 
24  to respond to the discovery requests, King asks the Court to enter a protective order containing 
25                                                                        

26  1 Both sides disagree over what occurred during the parties’ meet and confer efforts leading up to 
27  the instant motion.  Given the parties’ differing interpretations of that process, and the fact that 
   the motion is now before the Court, the Court declines to decide the issue on the parties meet and 
1  King’s proposed language.  King asserts that Defendants’ proposed language—which mandates 
2  specific sanctions for violations of the protective order and concludes that monetary remedies 
3  would be inadequate—is inappropriate.                                 
4       Defendants Michael and Adam Kaplan (the “Kaplan Defendants”) respond and counter-
5  move for a protective order.  (ECF No. 35).  The Kaplan Defendants assert that a motion to 
6  compel is unnecessary because they have already agreed to respond to the discovery requests, but 
7  simply require a protective order to do so.  The Kaplan Defendants’ countermotion asks the Court 
8  to enter the Kaplan Defendants’ proposed language.  Defendant Pure Water Technologies joins 
9  the Kaplan Defendants’ response and counter-motion.  (ECF No. 36).  King replies and reiterates 
10  that his version of the protective order is proper.  (ECF No. 39).  King also reiterates that 
11  sanctions are warranted because of Defendants’ last minute request for a protective order.   
12  II.  Legal standard.                                                  
13       If a party resists discovery, Rule 37(a) authorizes the requesting party to file a motion to 
14  compel.  The party resisting discovery bears the burden of showing why that discovery should not 
15  be permitted because it is irrelevant, overly broad, or unduly burdensome.  Fosbre v. Las Vegas 
16  Sands Corp., No. 2:10-cv-00765-APG-GWF, 2016 WL 54202, at *4 (D. Nev. Jan. 5, 2016).  If 
17  the court grants a motion to compel, the court must require the party whose conduct necessitated 
18  the motion, the party’s attorney, or both to pay the movant’s fees.  Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(a)(5)(A).   
19       Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(c) governs protective orders.  Blanket protective 
20  orders are (typically) stipulated agreements between the parties that generally require discovery to 
21  be conducted in a certain manner or be kept confidential.  See Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c)(1)(B); see 
22  Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation v. Lewis, No. 2:10-cv-00439-JCM-VCF, 2015 WL 
23  13667215, at *1 (D. Nev. July 29, 2015).  Blanket protective orders are designed to expedite the 
24  discovery process by permitting litigants to freely exchange sensitive information without the risk 
25  of disclosures.  Id.                                                  
26                                                                        
27                                                                        
1  III.  Discussion.                                                     
2       A.   King’s motion to compel.                                    
3       The Court denies King’s motion to compel because the Defendants have indicated that 
4  they are not refusing to respond to discovery requests (indeed, they have identified the Bates 
5  numbers of the documents they will produce) they are simply waiting until the parties have 
6  agreed on a protective order.  Because the Court determines the language of that protective order 
7  here, a motion to compel is not necessary.  The Court will, however, require Defendants to 
8  produce their responsive documents by November 17, 2023.              
9       B.   The Kaplan Defendants’ countermotion for a protective order.   
10       The Court grants in part and denies in part the Kaplan Defendants’ countermotion for a 
11  protective order.  Having reviewed both parties’ proposed language, the Court will require that 
12  the parties’ stipulated protective order contain King’s proposed language.  The Court does not 
13  find it necessary to dictate particular sanctions in the blanket protective order.  
14                                                                        
15       IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that King’s motion to compel (ECF No. 31) is denied.  
16       IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that Defendants’ responses to King’s requests for 
17  production identified in his motion to compel are due on or before November 17, 2023.  
18       IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the Kaplan Defendants’ countermotion for a 
19  protective order (ECF No. 35) is granted in part and denied in part.  It is granted in part 
20  regarding the Kaplan Defendants’ request that the Court order the parties to enter a protective 
21  order.  It is denied in part regarding the Kaplan Defendants’ request that the Court order the 
22  parties to include the Kaplan Defendants’ proposed language.          
23       IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the parties must incorporate King’s proposed 
24  language into a stipulated protective order and submit that order to the Court on or before 
25  December 4, 2023.                                                     
26       DATED: November 6, 2023                                          
27                                                                        
                                      DANIEL J. ALBREGTS
